what: Option Care Health is the largest independent provider of home and alternate-site infusion services in the United States. It delivers intravenous drugs - antibiotics, nutrition, immunoglobulin, specialty biologics - to patients at home or in its own infusion suites, with nurses and pharmacists supporting the treatment.
customers: Patients with chronic and acute conditions, paid for mainly by commercial health insurers, with smaller shares from Medicare and Medicaid. Referrals come from hospitals and physicians.
money: Long-term infusions such as immunoglobulin, specialty biologics and therapies for rare diseases.
Short courses such as antibiotics and nutrition after a hospital stay.
moat: National scale with local pharmacies and nursing, contracts with most large insurers, and the ability to handle complex specialty drugs that smaller providers cannot.
risks: Revenue is dominated by drug pass-through, so margins are thin and depend on payer reimbursement terms.
Changes to the price or competition for a few high-cost drugs can move results.
Large payers and pharmacy benefit managers own competing infusion businesses.
opportunities: Moving infusions out of hospitals into the home saves insurers money, a long-term tailwind.
Growth in specialty and rare-disease therapies keeps expanding the market.
watch: Gross profit per patient in chronic therapies. Revenue growth flatters the business because of drug prices; gross profit growth shows the real progress.
view: Revenue has risen from $3.4 billion in 2021 to $5.8 billion over the last twelve months, but net margin is only about 3.7%. That gap explains how to read Option Care: most of the revenue is the cost of expensive drugs passing through, and what the company really sells is the service of getting those drugs into a patient’s arm safely at home. Judged on gross profit and cash flow rather than revenue, it is a solid, growing healthcare services business, not a high-growth one.

The structural argument is strong. An infusion at home costs insurers far less than the same treatment in a hospital outpatient department, and both patients and payers prefer it. Option Care is the largest independent operator, which matters because the alternatives are owned by insurers and pharmacy benefit managers who are also its customers. That independence is a selling point to payers who do not want to hand more business to a competitor.

At about 23 times earnings, with the average analyst target slightly below the share price, the market already credits most of this. The risk is concentration in a few high-cost therapies whose economics can change when biosimilars or new competitors arrive. I would call the shares fairly priced: a dependable compounder in an attractive niche, but one where buying requires accepting a full multiple for a thin-margin business.
bull: Site-of-care shifts and new specialty therapies keep gross profit growing at double digits while buybacks shrink the share count.
bear: Reimbursement pressure or competition on a few large therapies squeezes thin margins, and payer-owned infusion businesses take share.
